title: It's MinneSOta, Not MinnesoTA
excerpt: I've moved to the Fond du Lac Reservation in Minnesota!
content:
After a year of doing absolutely nothing career-wise, I finally have a sleep schedule again because...

I got a job!!!

In a frenzy of post-resolution energy and hitherto unknown zeal, I applied to an AmeriCorps position as a Fond du Lac Reservation Food Sovereignty VISTA. Less than a month later I was on the road, starting a 2,000 mile road trip to the Land of 10,000 Lakes.

I haven't seen a single bit of wildlife yet as I've barely stepped out of my room (window views are more than enough in this sort of weather), but fresh deer tracks criss-crossing the backyard every morning tell me this place will be alive in spring.

So, that's how I've ended up in a rustic, little, snow-topped cabin filled with quaintly adorable 70s fixtures and honest-to-god well water coming out of my taps. My eyelashes have frozen together some mornings and sometimes my nostrils crackle with ice if I breathe in too deep, but am I happy and excited for the year to come?

You betcha!

❄️ ❄️ ❄️

title: Visiting The Matterhorn
excerpt: Faber and I continued our Switzerland adventures with a camping trip to see the Matterhorn last week!
content:
Faber and I continued our Switzerland adventures with a camping trip to see the Matterhorn last week! We spent two days and two nights roughing it up in the wilds of downtown Zermatt (and spent $70 to sleep on the ground :| ). Our first day and night were overcast and drizzly, but we managed to catch sight of the Matterhorn from our tent on the second afternoon!

Getting There

The train ride over was a typical Swiss journey—full of raging alpine rivers, craggy Alps' valleys, thundering waterfalls, and so much greenery!

The Hike: 5 Lakes Trail

Due to the weather and laziness levels, we were only able to go on one hike, the 5-Seenweg trail, otherwise known as the 5 Lakes! Clockwise from left, we have: Stellisee, Grindjisee, Grünsee, and Moosjisee! Unfortunately, Leisee is missing because I totally forgot to snap a photo (it wasn't very photogenic).

We saw glaciers, the aftermath of rock slides, crumbling chalets, and giant billowing clouds on every peak. The Matterhorn peeped out just as we reached the trailhead for the hike and accompanied us the whole way through.

Flora & Fauna

The trail was full of little critters and alpine plants! We saw purple crocuses (that grew like weeds everywhere!), tadpoles, frogs, a possible juvenile Golden Eagle (!!!), alpine succulents, a black squirrel (spot it in the middle of the top right photo!), gnarled stone pines, and—my absolute favorite—sweet little patches of alpine bellflowers!

❄️ We'll be back to see the Matterhorn in it's full winter splendor! ❄️

title: Drinking In the Views of Évian-les-Bains, France
excerpt: Faber and I went on a little international day trip to Evian, France this weekend!
content:
Faber and I went on a little international day trip to Evian, France this weekend!

The trip into Evian was quick but eventful! We took a bus into Morges, caught a boat to Ouchy Port in Lausanne, and then hopped onto a bigger ferry that took us straight to Evian. It cost about 15 CHF each one-way, 30 roundtrip, and 60 total for the two of us. Not the cheapest, but at least we got three boat rides out of it!

Food à La Française

Of course, the first thing we had to do was eat! I was on a mission to find foie gras, and we found it at Restaurant la Pizza. It came with toast, perfectly sweet candied onions, balsamic vinegar, and salt. I wasn't sure what I was expecting, but the foie gras was basically like a thick, meat flavored butter that really needed the toppings in order to work. I also had carbonara, Faber had pizza, and we both enjoyed a carafe of pure eau d'Evian. After a month in Switz, the bill was shockingly low at 40 euros. We considered the possibility of boating over every day for lunches.

Things to Do

After lunch, we visited the old Pump Room, which has unfortunately been converted into an Evian storefront selling bottled waters. Buuut, if you walk up the hill behind the building, you can find the Source Cachat, a darling little mosaic fountain of free Evian water! We filled up our water bottles and set off to explore the rest of the city.

We rode the famous funiculaire to the top of the town, got lost looking for the lake view, and rode all the way back down. It's a charmingly old, rickety ride to take, made all the better knowing that people have been sitting in the same seats since before WWI. Also, it's free!

We people-watched, ate some homemade gelato, and left just as storm clouds started rolling in. It was a perfect summer day to spend exploring Evian!

title: Hiking Grindelwald, Switzerland
excerpt: 🇨🇭 It doesn't get anymore Swiss than this 🇨🇭
content:
We finally arrived to Switzerland about a week ago, after a lot of uncertainty regarding visa restrictions in this mid-pandemic world. Traveling from London to Geneva by train with four giant pieces of luggage was...an inspiration to try out minimalism, to say the least!

It was worth it though, because Faber's parents took us on a lovely trip up to Grindelwald, where I got my first experience of German Switzerland!

The Hike

Of course, the trip's main event was a hike up to to Lake Bachalpsee and, oh my goodness, was it an adventure to be had! We cheated and took a gondola lift up (32 CHF each 😱), which left us at the iconic First Cliff Walk.

After a bit of sightseeing at First Station, we started on the nice, hour-long hike to the lake. Or at least, it would've been nice if the COVID lockdown hadn't turned me into a total slug. I was out of breath within ten minutes, although Faber with his soccer training was just fine.

The lake itself was beautiful, as it was a shade of icy teal and surrounded by giant, green peaks. Of course, it was further helped along by a gorgeous backdrop of the Alps, with perfect views of the Eiger, Jungfrau, Monch, and others. We dipped our toes into the glacier lake, but it was way too cold to stay in for long. Honestly, I've never had such a beautiful hike finale in my life!

The hike down was a little toooo long, but we survived. Never underestimate the price of Swiss transport, because it gets expen$$$ive. We found out the hard way, as we were planning on taking a 30-min. bus back down the mountain. Turns out that thirty minute ride would have cost us 46 CHF for the both of us, in cash! Needless to say, we didn't take it, but we did get some amazing pictures instead!

It was a trip for the books and a perfect introduction to the Swiss Alps. I think I'm starting to see what all the fuss is about!

title: Discovering Kew Gardens, London
excerpt: Rambling through England's botanical jewel known as Kew Gardens, featuring a particularly showy peacock!
content:
As lockdown restrictions have started lifting up in England (for better or worse), Faber and I have been able to visit Kew Gardens twice! Honestly, there is not enough time in the world to spend at this park, there's literally 326 acres of constantly changing flowers, trees, and insects in this little bubble of international botanicals. I have absolutely, completely fallen in love with Kew and their little gift shops. This place is a must visit whenever in London!

Waterlily House

This little greenhouse cottage is home to a tropical pond of giant water lilies (Victoria amazonica) and some gorgeously exotic lotus blooms (Nelumbo nucifera). This is hands-down my favorite spot in the entire park, it's so warm and colorful, the complete opposite of England's cold and rainy summer weather. It's like stepping into a lush pocket of sunshine and happiness!

Great Pagoda

There's no shortage of stunning blooms and gorgeous architecture in the park, and the Great Pagoda area is no exception. We got breathtaking shots with a resident peacock, who was even gracious enough to shake out his tail feathers and give us a show!

The Rose Garden & Palm House

Flanked by beds upon beds of roses and a row of patriotic statues, Palm House is another one of Kew's greenhouse marvels. Unbeknownst to us, we visited at just the right times to see pretty much everything in full bloom, so we had lots of selfie opportunities!

Palm House itself is like a smaller version of Temperate House and, of course, focuses on the world's palm species. The inner structure work features spiral staircases and beautiful metal detailing.

Temperate House

Kew's most iconic spot, T.H. is apparently the world's largest Victorian greenhouse. We didn't get to see much due to COVID restrictions, but what we did see had us captivated. It's a lovely place and—conveniently—an actual wedding venue (#Riverstaffe2023)!!!

Kew Blooms

I think the best thing about the park is being able to see flowers and plants from literally opposite ends of the Earth planted right next to each other, perfectly cared for and beautifully arranged. It's pretty fair to say that you don't go out to visit Kew—you're really going in to a explore a whole new world!

title: Quarantining in the English Countryside
excerpt: What it's been like quarantining in a 16th-century English manor.
content:
Faber and I have been lucky to spend our British quarantine at his friend's apartment, which just so happens to be part of a giant 16th century manor house on the outskirts of London, UK.

The Grounds

The garden is full of flowers I've never seen before, a walkway lined with English oaks, a pair of giant stone gazebos, and—of course—a huge fountain right in the middle of it all!

I've tried identifying the garden and wild flowers as accurately as possible; however, anything with an asterisk is a plant I'm unsure about, either due to being possible hybrids or sheer genus variety!

From left: 1. *Maiden Pink Hybrid, Dianthus deltoides. 2. Rose Campion, Lychnis coronaria ‘Alba'. 3. Red Hot Poker, Kniphofia uvaria. 4. *Rhododendron with bumblebee, Rhododendron

Beyond the Wall

Leaving the garden, the property is surrounded by fields that are teeming with wildflowers, old-growth trees, rabbits, butterflies, deer, and⁠ teeny tiny frogs!

From left: 1. Elderberry, Sambucus nigra. 2. Foxglove, Digitalis purpurea. 3. *Slender Speedwell, Veronica filiformis. 4. *Field Rose, Rosa arvensis.

From left: 1. Blue Atlas Cedar, Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca'. 2. Tulip Tree, Liriodendron tulipifera. 3. English Oak, Quercus robur.

But of course, it wouldn't be England without the rain, and we've been having A LOT of it.

I don't think we could have spent quarantine in a better place.

title: Saying Annyeong to Seoul
excerpt: It's bittersweet, but Faber and I are getting ready to say goodbye to Korea this week.
content:
It's bittersweet, but Faber and I are getting ready to say goodbye to Korea this week. Our teaching contracts are up, plane tickets purchased, and suitcases are getting packed. Despite everything going on with corona, we're still getting to see our friends and keeping life as normal as possible. In fact, now that work is over and we can just have fun, I'm starting to regret leaving!

We'll be back for our friends (and to load up on kimchi and BBQ) but it's time to go and make more memories. As Faber so perfectly put it: "It's the end of the chapter, not the book." And it wouldn't really be that great of a book if we never changed the setting, now would it?

So, annyeong, Korea! I will always have these two years worth of fun, food, and friends in my heart. Don't miss us too much though—we'll be back and irritating Itaewon's bouncers in no time at all 😜.

title: A Week in Ho Chi Minh, Vietnam
excerpt: Merry Vietmas from Ho Chi Minh! A seven day Christmas trip in Vietnam.
content:
After teaching my little kindergarteners for a year with barely a break to be had, Faber, a friend, and I headed to Ho Chi Minh for some fun in the warm, warm sun! Seoul winters are horrible and we managed to disappear just in time to avoid the coldest December temps. HCMC was hot, humid, and bursting with tourists and food; it was literally everything we'd been craving since the end of Korea's summer 💖

Food Around the City

Hands down, the absolute best spot we stumbled on was Hanoi Day, a teeny little place in the Cafe Apartment building in HCMC's Time Square. We went back there at least three times, and ordered the exact same thing each visit: fresh guava tea (orange juice for Faber), giant spring rolls, and a sweet pork dish with wide, paper thin folds of rice noodles. Each visit was just as good as the last—and the best part?? The total bill came to just over ten dollars for both us every time. Starting off the day there basically had us set until dinner. Plus, the interior is adorable, earthy, and relaxing. I absolutely loved it ❤️.

Honestly, the best part of our trip was the food. Hanoi Day was my fave, but I also ate my weight in fried duck, vermicelli, peanut sauce, and cocktails around the city. Surprisingly (and kind of regretfully) we only had pho and bánh mì once, but there were just so many things to try!

Culture and Museums

When not gorging ourselves on food, Faber and I managed to see some historical sights around the city! The War Remnants Museum, although busy, really was a must and it made for an informative (if sad) afternoon. The Saigon Central Post Office was a nice little souvenir spot right next door to the Notre Dame Cathedral of Saigon. HCMC has gorgeous tropical flowers all over and I loved finding little oases of frangipani and lotuses in random spots around the city.

Bazaars and Street Markets

We were able to find two little street markets that were filled with handmade knickknacks and street snacks. We had some gorgeous henna done, saw some fried scorpions, and bought a bunch of hand-crocheted keychains. These markets were highlights of the trip.

Bui Vien is not Muy Bien

We loved most parts of our trip, but there's no denying Vietnam is still very much a developing country. There were definitely some run-down places that felt a little unsafe, but for the most part we really enjoyed ourselves. One part we absolutely disliked was Bùi Viện Street, which is super famous for its clubs. We were excited to visit, but, unfortunately, there's a lot of child street performers and moms with literal infants standing outside clubs blaring insane volumes of music until early hours of the morning. It put a big damper on the night to see kids my siblings' age performing for money late at night :(. It's hard because HCMC thrives off tourism and it's really heartbreaking to see poverty like that first hand. Regardless, the country itself is beautiful, the food is amazing, and the people were kind. It's definitely a trip we won't soon forget!

title: Traveling Tokyo 2019
excerpt: How we spent four days eating perfectly boiled eggs, picking up souvenirs, and more.
content:
After visiting Japan for the first time last year, Faber and I have been dying to go back every spare weekend we have ! We finally managed to find the time with our Chuseok holiday, which is the Korean version of American Thanksgiving. We spent four glorious days eating perfectly boiled eggs, picking up souvenirs, and just enjoying the bustling neat-and-tidiness that is Tokyo.

Things We Did (and Ate)

1. Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden

We spent a gorgeous afternoon strolling through the Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden . Admission was only about $5 each and it's a huge park, so it's easy to spend a whole day there. Unbeknownst to us, there were tons of spots to picnic and relax, so we had to piece together a makeshift blanket from our raincoats. Honestly, this a great thing to do after a night of Strong Zeros, Japan's conbini answer to cheap drinks in the form of a 9% highball-in-a-can for about $2~ (which I also HIGHLY recommend).

2. Food

It's true, arguably the best thing about Japan is the food. Although Faber tends to go with a more devil-may-care attitude and likes walking into any random spot when hungry, I must admit that we haven't really had a bad meal on either of our trips. Restaurant bills can get pricey, but we don't mind paying up when it's as good as this!

Clockwise from left: 1. Earl grey bubble tea from a pop-up spot in Shibuya. 2. A customized ginger pork dish with like 4 extra raw and soft boiled eggs from Sukiya, a chain that we absolutely adore. 3. I didn't get a pretty picture, but this ramen bowl was hands-down the best meal of the trip, and it was one of Faber's cavalier, hangry choices to boot. We will definitely be visiting this spot again. 4. The legendary fluffy pancakes I'd been dying to try for months, from Banks Cafe. Topped with berries, ice cream, whipped cream, and chocolate sauce, they were as delicious as they looked and were about $15!!! 5. Fatty tuna and salmon sushi from a random, delicious place near our AirBnB.

3. Exploring the City

This trip was pretty much a Shibuya-only adventure, and there was more than enough to keep us occupied for four days. Walking around the neighborhood is fun enough alone, and we loved going into the shops and touristy alleys. We did venture out to DisneySea for a daytrip, which I wrote more about here, and loved every second of it.

All in all, the holiday was over in the blink of an eye (or slurp of a ramen bowl) and we left with dragging feet and a few extra pounds after another memorable Tokyo trip 💖.

title: Tokyo DisneySea - Chuseok 2019
excerpt: Faber and I spent our Chuseok holiday on an impromptu trip to DisneySea this year!
content:
Faber and I spent our Chuseok holiday on an impromptu trip to Tokyo this year! The trade war between SK and Japan made tickets super cheap, so we decided to head over on one condition: we'd finally get to visit DisneySea!!!

Honestly, I LOVED this park!!! I've seen it described as an adult version of the other parks, and I definitely agree. It felt way bigger than Disneyland and California Adventure (my only other references haha). There was so much going on, and the scenery and architectural details were gorgeous. There was a little Europe section, Arabian Coast, Mermaid Lagoon, Aztec temples, an Old Americana spot—just a little bit of everything and it was all sooo pretty! Even Faber had to agree the Mediterranean area was great.

My absolute favorite area was Mermaid Lagoon. The decorations, buildings, general atmosphere—they were all a fever dream come true for inner five-year-old me.

t

The worst part of the day was food. We had lunch/dinner at Volcania in Mysterious Island, and it was nothing special. In fact, we couldn't even finish our meals, which was a shame because they were quite pricey (Disney inflation, amirite?). Volcania itself was super interesting, with an underwater lab/grotto look. I did try out a limited edition Mickey Mummy bun, however, which ended up being really tasty.

The day's peak event came early on when I managed to convince Faber into purchasing matching his-and-hers ears. We got Duffy and Shellie ears, a DisneySea exclusive item. I'd never heard of Duffy pre-Japan!

title: Hiking Mt. Fuji
excerpt: A summer hike up Mt. Fuji - a trip report.
content:
July 24, 2018 - Tech Specs

It's been a while since I hiked Mt. Fuji, and I didn't particularly enjoy it at the time, but I love looking back on the pictures I took. We took the Yoshida trail, slept in the Taishikan Hut at 8th station, and summited by sunrise on July 25th. This was my first "real" hike and I wore five layers throughout the climb: a Uniqlo Airism tee, Uniqlo Heat-tech long sleeve, Patagonia Synchilla, Patagonia Nano Air jacket, and a Patagonia Torrentshell. I also wore Heat-tech leggings, fleece-lined/water-repellant tights, and Danner Mountain Light boots. I carried my gear in a Fjallraven Kanken, but I wouldn't recommend it; the straps began to dig in too much mid-hike and were quite uncomfortable. My clothing layers were not enough and I can't stress how cold it gets up there. It's an easy hike but make sure you prepare or I promise you will be miserable! I definitely was. Anyway, here is my trip report!

10 a.m. - Ascent

Faber and I arrived at Mt. Fuji's Fifth Station from Tokyo's Shinjuku at 10 a.m. the day of the hike. I think this gave us the perfect amount of time to hike slowly and comfortably (I was definitely not fit by any means). We bought a short little souvenir stick, paid in cash, at one of the shops located on Fifth and then began the hike by eleven a.m. The first few miles consisted of endless, metal covered switchbacks with a touch of rock scrambling at points, but the path was relatively clear and quiet. I was exhausted by 11:30 a.m.

5 p.m. - Mountain Hut

We arrived at our home for the night by 5 p.m. and got settled in quickly. I was expecting some sort of private capsule room since we paid about 80 USD each in cash, but we were totally shocked to discover that we were in a giant sleeping hall lined with what were essentially human-sized shelves! We just got sleeping bags and a spot next to each other in one of the huge wall bunks. Any ideas of a reinvigorating sleep before the final ascent went out the window as we hunkered down amid chatting couples, flashing lamps, and tired kids. The toilets were basic and pay-to-enter (cash), and the snacks and curry we got on arrival were gone in seconds. We did get some nice pics above the cloud line, though.

2 a.m. - Final Ascent

After a night of no sleep, we got up (along with everyone else) in order to climb the final leg. Honestly, this was the worst part. Mountain weather is no joke, and even though we thought we had prepared (we were basically kitted out in Patagonia layers), the wind and light drizzle that drove right into our faces was miserable. Since there were so many people, there was also an actual line to hike up the mountain, and we were essentially in stop-and-go foot traffic at several points along the way. We always felt safe though, as there where guides with lights and safety vests lining the path every few minutes.

4 a.m. - Summit

We managed to make it to the top of the mountain just before sunrise and found a good spot overlooking the mountain edge. Alas, all our efforts came to naught as the sun decided to hide behind a thick layer of clouds that morning and temps remained freezing. We ducked into a shelter, ate some snacks and tried desperately to warm up. Unfortunately, we didn't, and Faber insisted on beginning our descent.

5 a.m. - Descent

Honestly, the descent would have been uneventful if it weren't for the fact that the trail is made up of loose volcanic gravel and powdery soil. I felt like I was going to break my ankles walking too quickly but I also wanted gravity to help me work less since it was a pretty sharp decline. All in all, we took about 5 hours to hike back down, all while wiping black eye and nose gunk off our faces due to the clouds of dust we kicked up walking. We were quite happy to be done and excited to head over to our ryokan in Fujikawaguchiko later that day!

I'm happy we crossed Mt. Fuji off our list, but the proverb really is true: "“A wise man climbs Mt. Fuji once, only a fool climbs it twice." Pictures will be enough for the rest of our lives~~~

title: Everland, South Korea
excerpt: Backstage passes into Everland, one of South Korea's biggest theme parks!
content:
One of the first outings I did once moved into Seoul, was visit the Everland theme park!!! Spring-time Everland is gorgeous and Faber and I had a wonderful time walking through the park's gigantic, over the top flower displays and quaint, Euro-themed decor. There was so much to do and see, including an animal safari, the world's 4th steepest rollercoaster, and photo-ops galore.

I had no expectations going into the park as we had gotten last-minute freebie tickets with friends and it was our first time getting out Seoul, but it was an amazing daytrip that we absolutely recommend! The park was packed, but we managed to do everything thanks to our friends' backstage access.

Despite the ethicalities of having wild creatures at a for-profit theme park, the main draw here is definitely the animals. We saw pandas, white tigers, elephants, giant bears—everything you can think of safari-wise is here and on display. We felt a bit guilty watching brown bears do spins and tricks for treats, and some of the bigger ape species definitely seemed under-stimulated, but the enclosures we saw appeared maintained and cared for. Regardless, this is not a zoo, and a one time visit was enough for us.

After touring the animal area, we explored the rides and foods. The most popular rollercoaster here is the T-Express, and we were lucky enough to skip the lines and ride it a couple times back-to-back. It's a terrifying ride that literally took my breath away, I don't know how I managed to do it twice!

Anyway, Everland was an adorable, exciting way to spend a Saturday. Pro-tip, though: find a friend who works there so you can escape the insane ride lines!
